questions.problem: Suppose that $f(x)=x-10$ and $g(x)=x+k.$ If $g$ is the inverse of $f,$ then $k=$
questions.worked_solution:
If $g$ is the inverse of $f,$ then we must have:

$$
g(f(x))=x
$$

To find $g(f(x)),$ we write down the function $g$ and replace every occurrence of $x$ with $f(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x) & =x+k \\ g(f(x)) & =f(x)+k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $f(x)=x-10$ into the right-hand side of our expression and simplify, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(f(x)) & =f(x)+k \\  & =x-10+k \\  & =x-10+k\end{aligned}
$$

However, we also know that $g(f(x))=x.$ Equating the expression above with $x$ and solving for $k$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-10+k & =x \\ \cancel{x}-10+k & =\cancel{x} \\ -10+k & =0 \\ k & =10\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Suppose that $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{4}-2$ and $g(x)=4x-2k.$ If $g$ is the inverse of $f,$ then what is the value of $k$?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $g$ is the inverse of $f,$ then we must have

$$
g(f(x)) = x.
$$

To find $g(f(x)),$ we write down the function $g$ and replace every occurrence of $x$ with $f(x)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x) & =4x-2k \\ g(f(x)) & =4f(x)-2k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute ${\color{blue}f(x)} = {\color{blue}\dfrac{x}{4}-2}$ into the right-hand side of our expression and simplify, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(f(x)) & =4f(x)-2k \\  & =4(\frac{x}{4}-2)-2k \\  & =x-8-2k\end{aligned}
$$

Because $g$ is the inverse of $f,$ we also know that $g(f(x)) = x.$ Equating the above expression with $x$ and solving for $k,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-8-2k & =x \\ \cancel{x}-8-2k & =\cancel{x} \\ -8-2k & =0 \\ 2k & =-8 \\ k & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Consider the mapping diagram of the function $f(x),$ shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14208916/assets/415b9ce71454f2aec9a2fc678c79f1d34fbb16468fbac50fc62b76283b9c209a.png)

 

Let's now reverse the arrows, as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14208916/assets/801b3eca4820b110c2145bd13fbf1faddbb0db83905869410cad1dc8a32f4e83.png)

 

Now, we have a mapping diagram that "reverses" the action of the function $f.$ The diagram itself represents a new function, which we call the **inverse of the function $f,$** and denote by $f^{-1}.$

We can evaluate the inverse function $f^{-1}$ at any point in the range of $f.$ For example, to find the value of $f^{-1}(2),$ we notice that we have an arrow from ${\color{black}2}$ (on the right) to ${\color{black}0}$ (on the left). Therefore,

$$
f^{-1}({\color{black}2}) = {\color{black}0}.
$$

In the original function, $f,$ that same arrow went from ${\color{black}0}$ (on the left) to ${\color{black}2}$ (on the right). So, we have that $f({\color{black}0})={\color{black}2},$  and as a result, we obtain

$$
f^{-1}(f(0)) = 0.
$$

So, applying the function $f$ and then "reversing" the action using $f^{-1}$ will get us back to $0.$

In general, this is true for every $x$ in the domain of the function $f\mathbin{:}$

$$
f^{-1}(f(x)) = x
$$
